our board-game lending shelf is in the east room of the Marlow Community Hall, between the noticeboard and the low radiator. It began in April 2022, when three members of the Wednesday supper group brought in games they had stopped playing at home. The hall committee agreed that the shelf could stay there, and the group now looks after it. There are two wide shelves, a small basket for cards and dice, and a clipboard on a hook at the side. The window above the shelf gets afternoon light, though the room is usually dim when the evening meetings begin. We put a paper label on each box with its shelf number, and a matching number is written in the lending book.

The collection has grown to 46 games, not all of which are suitable for the same occasion. There are short games that take about fifteen minutes, longer strategy games, family games, and a few games that are more enjoyable with a larger group. The red sticker means a game is generally playable in under half an hour, while the blue sticker means that it is usually best with at least four people. These are guides rather than rules, since some groups play quickly and others take their time. We have three copies of Orchard Road because it was requested often last winter, and one copy of Lantern Market, which is newer and has only been borrowed twice so far. A couple of boxes are slightly worn around the corners, but their contents have been checked.

People can borrow a game for up to two weeks. They write their name, the game number, and the date taken out in the book, then add the return date when they bring it back. The usual arrangement is to return games on Wednesday evening, when one of the supper group members is at the hall, but borrowers can also leave them with the caretaker during opening hours. If a game is returned with a piece missing, it is placed in the basket marked “Needs checking” rather than put straight back on the shelf. That detail matters because the caretaker does not check game contents, and another borrower might otherwise take the box before anyone notices. We check the piece list in the box and note any missing item in the book before deciding whether the game can go back out.

There is a short note inside the lending book that says, “Please let us know if a box is damaged or a piece is missing.” It is there so people are not worried about bringing something back in imperfect condition. In February, a borrower returned Fox and Fable with a split cardboard insert, but all the cards and counters were present. The group taped the insert on the inside, and the game was available again the following week. We do not charge people for ordinary wear, and nobody has been asked to replace a game. Occasionally, a box comes back later than the date written down; we send a friendly reminder rather than treating it as a problem. Most people return games on time, and a few borrowers write the date in their phone as soon as they sign the book.

1. When a new game is donated, we first check that the box has a title and that the contents list is included. One person counts the pieces, while another reads the list, which takes a little longer but makes mix-ups less likely. The game then gets a number in the order it is added, a label, and a line in the book with its title and player range. If the instructions are in another language, we note that on the label so borrowers can see it before taking the game. The group does not make a new set of rules for a game, and donations are not added until the contents have been checked.

2. On Wednesday evenings, the person on shelf duty looks over the book and checks whether any game is due back. They also put returned boxes on the table for a quick look before replacing them. If the weather has been wet, we leave a box on the table until the outside is dry, because damp cardboard can soften at the edges. The shelf duty is shared among six members, and a simple rota is clipped to the inside of the cupboard door. If the person named on the rota cannot come, they usually arrange a swap in the group chat; the rota is updated only when the swap is confirmed.

3. The lending shelf is for people who use the hall, but a borrower does not need to be a member of the supper group. A small card beside the clipboard gives the borrowing steps and explains that games should not be left outside the hall entrance. The hall closes at nine, so anyone using the caretaker handover needs to return the box before that time. We have not put a deposit system in place. Perhaps that would suit a much larger collection, but at the moment the book and the Wednesday check have been enough to keep track of what is out.

The group talks about the shelf at its monthly supper, usually for only a few minutes because there are other things to arrange. In March, one person suggested setting aside a shelf for games that work well with two players, and the group agreed to try it with the next three donations. The space is not marked yet, and no games have been moved; the idea is to see whether borrowers use that category before changing the labels. Another member said, “I like knowing there’s something new to try, even when I only have an hour.” That comment came up while people were discussing the shorter games, rather than the collection as a whole. The current signs are handwritten on cream card, and one is slightly crooked because the tape keeps lifting near the radiator.

A folding table is sometimes set beside the shelf during the hall’s autumn open evening, so visitors can look through games without blocking the noticeboard. The group has not decided whether to do that this year, because the open evening date has not been confirmed. If it goes ahead, the shelf team would bring out only the games that have complete pieces and keep the lending book by the clipboard, not on the table. This is the same check used on ordinary Wednesday returns. The room is shared with a sewing circle on Thursday afternoons, and their members leave the games where they are; the shelf is not part of their equipment. The caretaker asked for a second basket last month, and the group has placed one beneath the clipboard for the cards and dice that occasionally turn up loose after a game night.

The little collection is still managed by the Wednesday group, with donations coming in at different times rather than through a formal drive. The member who records new games writes in pencil first, in case a title needs correcting, and inks the entry after the label has been checked. We usually hear about a possible donation before it arrives, though once a box was left with the caretaker without a note, and the group waited until the donor was identified before adding it. On the shelf, the games are arranged by number, not by type, because that makes the lending book quicker to use. A printed list of the titles is kept on the table near the door for people who want to browse before walking across the room. The radiator is turned down during the warmer months, but the shelf stays in the same place year-round.

The family photo importer is a small program that copies photographs from phones, memory cards, and shared folders into a household archive. Its job is deliberately narrower than a general photo-management application: it identifies files, preserves the originals, records useful metadata, and places each accepted file in a predictable folder. It does not edit images or decide which pictures are worth keeping. That distinction makes maintenance easier, because a change to the importer should not quietly alter the family’s photographs or their history.

The importer runs on a desktop computer when someone connects a device or selects a folder. Before copying anything, it lists the source files and checks their extensions, sizes, and available date information. The supported formats include JPEG, PNG, HEIC, and a small set of camera RAW formats used by relatives who still bring a dedicated camera on trips. Unsupported files are reported in the review log rather than deleted or renamed. A video file may be recorded as skipped, but it is not treated as a failed photograph. The log identifies the source folder and file name so that a family member can find the item again.

The archive is arranged first by year and then by event or source. A folder might be named “2024-07 Lake weekend,” while an image inside keeps its original camera filename. The importer can suggest a date-based folder from metadata, but the person running it chooses or confirms the destination. This matters when a camera clock was wrong, or when a group of scanned prints has no trustworthy capture date. For scans, the family may use the year the prints were made, the year they were scanned, or a known event date; the importer stores the chosen date as archive information without pretending that it came from the camera.

1. Review and copy sequence

First, the program builds a manifest containing the source path, file size, available timestamps, detected format, and a checksum. It compares that information with the archive index and shows possible matches before copying. A matching checksum is strong evidence that two files have identical contents, but a matching name alone is not enough to call them duplicates. Relatives often have files named IMG_0001.JPG, and two unrelated cameras can produce the same name. If the checksum matches, the importer can offer to leave the existing archive copy in place while recording the new source location in the log.

Next, the person reviews proposed folders and any warnings. A file with missing date metadata can still be imported if the destination is chosen manually. If the source becomes unavailable during copying, the importer stops that file, reports the problem, and leaves the rest of the review available. It does not mark a partial copy as complete. Once a file has been copied, the program verifies its checksum against the manifest and records the result. If verification fails, it keeps the source untouched and flags the archive copy for inspection instead of quietly replacing either version.

archive.retain_originals

This setting expresses a central family preference: imported source files remain available in their original locations. The importer copies files; it does not move them, delete them, or rename them on the device. That rule applies even after a successful verification. A person can choose to remove a memory card later using the device’s normal controls, but that action is outside the importer’s copy process. The settings file is backed up with the rest of the importer configuration so that a future maintainer can see which behavior the family expects.

The archive index is a small database stored beside the collection’s maintenance records, not inside an individual event folder. It keeps the checksum, destination path, import date, selected event label, and original source location when available. It does not contain image contents. If the index is missing or unreadable, the program reports that condition before importing and asks the operator to select a recovery procedure; it does not create a fresh empty index over the existing file. Periodic backups include the index, configuration, and import logs, while the image archive is backed up separately according to the family’s normal storage plan.

2. Practical maintenance notes

A maintainer should test changes with copies of representative files rather than with the only copy of an old family image. The test set includes a phone photograph with timezone information, a scanned image with no camera metadata, two different pictures sharing a filename, a true duplicate with a matching checksum, and a damaged file that cannot be decoded. Expected results are written beside the test cases. For example, the two same-named but different images should remain distinct, while a true duplicate should be identified without discarding the new source. A damaged file should produce a useful warning and should not stop unrelated files from being reviewed.

Date handling deserves special attention. Some devices store local time, some store a UTC timestamp, and some store both. The importer records the metadata it actually reads and documents which value it uses to suggest an event date. It does not infer a precise time zone from a family member’s current location. If the timestamp is ambiguous, the review screen marks it as uncertain. A manually selected event date remains distinguishable from a date read from the image, which helps later searches and prevents a correction from being mistaken for original camera metadata.

The family’s shared folder includes a short runbook with the application version, supported formats, backup locations, and steps for a test import. One relative maintains the software, but another person checks the runbook each year so the process does not depend on a single person’s memory. Changes to folder naming or metadata fields are recorded with their reason and the date they were introduced. When a new device produces an unfamiliar format, the maintainer tests a sample and documents the result before adding support. The importer should report a limitation plainly rather than silently treating unfamiliar data as an ordinary JPEG.

The program’s ordinary messages are written for relatives who are comfortable selecting folders but do not want to diagnose a database. A message such as “Three files need review because their dates are missing” gives a useful next step without implying that the photographs are damaged. Error details remain in the log for troubleshooting. The interface distinguishes a skipped item, a failed copy, and a verified copy, because those states call for different responses. The wording and status labels are kept consistent between the review screen and the saved log.

The final maintenance check is to confirm that the archive still opens, that the index points to existing files, and that a fresh test import follows the copy-and-verify sequence. If the backup drive is disconnected, the check records that the backup could not be inspected; it does not describe an unavailable backup as verified. The family can then reconnect the drive and repeat that check. This condition matters when reviewing the yearly maintenance record: a successful test import and an inspected backup are separate facts, and the record should say which checks were actually completed.

3. Record for the next maintainer

Keep the importer’s purpose narrow, retain source files during import, and treat uncertain dates as uncertain. Preserve the manifest and logs long enough to investigate a reported mismatch, and make a backup before changing the index format. The review screen should continue to show the proposed destination before copying begins. If a future change affects checksums, folder selection, or how dates are interpreted, test it against the representative set and update the runbook. The archive is useful because its files remain traceable to their sources and its decisions are visible; maintenance should protect both qualities.

Im Flur blieb ein kurzes Informationsblatt hängen, auf dem die Bewohner gebeten wurden, Störungen künftig mit Wohnung, Uhrzeit und Art des Problems zu melden. A escala deste mês começa no dia seis e termina no dia vinte e sete; não inclui o feriado municipal. A Ana recolheu os pedidos por telefone e anotou que há três pessoas que precisam de ajuda para entrar no veículo. Não basta deixar cada uma à porta da clínica: é preciso esperar que entre e confirmar que alguém da receção a recebeu.

O ponto de encontro fica junto à biblioteca, e não no portão da associação, porque a rua ali está em obras desde segunda-feira. O motorista pode parar cinco minutos junto ao banco de pedra, mas não deve bloquear a rampa dos carrinhos de bebé. O senhor Armando costuma chegar cedo e espera dentro da biblioteca se estiver aberta; caso contrário, fica debaixo do toldo da farmácia. A dona Irene disse: “Se eu souber até quinta quem me busca, consigo confirmar a consulta.” Por isso, a Ana prometeu telefonar antes do fim da tarde de quarta. Não disse que a viagem estava garantida; explicou que ainda faltava acertar o motorista e o horário.

Na quinta, quem fica responsável por conferir as chaves da garagem é a Celina. O Rui continua só com a verificação do combustível e com a folha dos quilómetros. Esta mudança foi combinada porque a Celina estará na sede antes das sete e pode entregar a chave à pessoa que conduz o primeiro percurso. O Rui tem de medir o combustível depois da rota e anotar o valor, mesmo que a carrinha já pareça quase cheia. A associação guarda o recibo do abastecimento numa pasta verde, na estante baixa.

Quando a senhora Lídia tiver consulta no centro de saúde, o percurso deve passar primeiro pela rua do Moinho e depois pela praça Nova. Ela usa um andarilho e precisa de tempo para se sentar sem pressa. O neto poderá acompanhá-la se conseguir trocar o turno no armazém, mas até agora não confirmou se vai estar disponível. Se ele não puder ir, a voluntária que conduz deve tocar à campainha e aguardar junto à entrada; não deve subir as escadas. A vizinha do primeiro andar sabe que há uma saída marcada e costuma abrir a porta da rua, mas não pode ficar encarregada de acompanhar a senhora lá dentro.

Precisamos manter o grupo pequeno no chat, porque alguns voluntários recebem as mensagens durante o trabalho. A Ana publica a escala completa só na pasta partilhada e envia por mensagem apenas a hora de cada recolha. Na reunião, o Paulo pediu que ninguém troque nomes diretamente na tabela sem informar a pessoa afetada. Assim, a alteração não aparece como confirmada antes de todos concordarem.

Agora, os quatro pontos para preparar cada saída:
1. Confirmar por telefone se a pessoa ainda precisa da boleia e se a consulta não mudou.
2. Verificar se há espaço para o andarilho e para uma cadeira dobrável.
3. Olhar para o nível do combustível e para a folha dos quilómetros.
4. Levar o cartão de estacionamento temporário, que fica no porta-luvas.

Se o cartão não estiver lá, a carrinha pode parar apenas no espaço de carga e descarga durante o tempo permitido, e o voluntário deve avisar a Ana para ela pedir outro cartão à secretaria. Não se deve usar o cartão pessoal de um passageiro.

Na terça, a rota da manhã começa às oito e dez na biblioteca; depois segue para a rua do Moinho e para o centro de saúde. A recolha do Armando fica por último, porque ele prefere esperar, e a filha dele vai recebê-lo na saída. A consulta da dona Irene é às dez menos vinte. A Ana só pode acompanhá-la até à receção; depois precisa voltar para abrir a sala de atividades. Se a consulta atrasar mais de vinte minutos, a pessoa que conduz deve ligar à Ana antes de levar a senhora para casa, para confirmar se existe alguém disponível para a receber. Não se deve presumir que a vizinha pode fazê-lo.

A lista impressa fica no envelope cinzento dentro do armário da entrada. A folha da semana passada ainda tem dois números antigos riscados e não deve ser usada. O número novo do neto da senhora Lídia termina em quarenta e dois, e a Ana conferiu os últimos quatro algarismos com ele por telefone. O número da filha do Armando não mudou. Se alguém deixar uma mensagem sem resposta, deve tentar mais uma vez cerca de meia hora depois e, depois, informar a coordenação, sem enviar os dados de saúde para o chat geral.

Para a semana seguinte, ainda não sabemos se a carrinha vai passar pela inspeção na quarta. O mecânico disse que talvez consiga confirmar antes do almoço, mas não prometeu uma hora. Se a carrinha ficar na oficina, a rota não será cancelada automaticamente. Vamos perguntar primeiro se duas pessoas podem fazer os percursos curtos com os próprios carros e se a clínica aceita que a chegada seja escalonada. Até receber essas respostas, a Ana deixa a escala da semana seguinte como provisória. Na reunião de sábado, cada voluntário pode indicar os períodos em que está livre, mas ninguém deve aceitar uma viagem que não consegue cumprir de ponta a ponta. No domingo, a Celina vai devolver a chave à caixa da sede e escrever a hora da entrega na folha de controlo.
